title: Homogeneous primary decomposition of a polynomial ideal, with localization data
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], $n\ge0$, and $B=k[x_0,\ldots,x_n]$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring] with its total-degree grading [def-pc-standard-graded-algebra]. Let $I\subseteq B$ be a homogeneous ideal, meaning that every homogeneous component of each element of $I$ lies in $I$. The ring $B$ is Noetherian, meaning every ideal is finitely generated. There are finitely many proper homogeneous ideals $Q_1,\ldots,Q_s$ such that $I=\bigcap_{a=1}^s Q_a$, each $Q_a$ is primary, the radicals $\mathfrak p_a=\sqrt{Q_a}$ are distinct homogeneous prime ideals, and this intersection is irredundant. Here primary means $uv\in Q_a$, $u\notin Q_a$ imply $v^h\in Q_a$ for some $h\ge1$; $\sqrt Q=\{b:b^h\in Q\text{ for some }h\ge1\}$. Every prime minimal among those containing $I$ occurs among the $\mathfrak p_a$. For every $a$ there is $h_a\ge1$ with $\mathfrak p_a^{h_a}\subseteq Q_a$. For every prime $\mathfrak p\supseteq I$, localization [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] gives
$$IB_{\mathfrak p}=\bigcap_{\mathfrak p_a\subseteq\mathfrak p}Q_aB_{\mathfrak p};$$
if $\mathfrak p_a\not\subseteq\mathfrak p$ then $Q_aB_{\mathfrak p}=B_{\mathfrak p}$. In particular if $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak p_b$ is minimal over $I$, then $IB_{\mathfrak p_b}=Q_bB_{\mathfrak p_b}$. The empty intersection is $B$, so $I=B$ is included with $s=0$.

source.place: Theorem 20.27, Appendix: Homogeneity, printed p.123; Exercises 20.25-20.26; primary localization in Chapter 18. Local PDF WANTED; read the authors online PDF https://web.mit.edu/18.705/www/13Ed.pdf. Stacks algebra.tex Tag 00JM (section-proj), homogeneous ideal and Proj conventions; the graded primary-decomposition assertion itself is the cited textbook theorem, not attributed to a Stacks tag.

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-polynomial-ring-field-regular-ring] with n+1 variables to obtain that B is Noetherian. If I=B, choose the empty family: its intersection is B, there is no prime containing I, and all other assertions are vacuous. Henceforth I is proper. By [lem-per-noetherian-primary-decomposition], write I as a finite intersection of proper primary ideals P_j; the family is nonempty because I is proper.

source.place: Theorem 20.27, first sentence of proof; Theorem 18.21, printed p.109.

proof.text: For each P_j take its homogeneous core H_j from [lem-sfb-primary-homogeneous-core]. The total-degree decomposition of B is a nonnegative grading and step 1 supplies Noetherianity. Thus H_j is proper, homogeneous and primary. If f lies in I, each component f_d lies in I and hence in P_j; the explicit core formula gives f in H_j. Conversely H_j is contained in P_j, so intersection_j H_j is contained in intersection_j P_j=I. Therefore I=intersection_j H_j.

For each H_j its radical p_j is a homogeneous ideal by [lem-sfb-homogeneous-ideal-radical]. It is proper since 1^h=1 cannot belong to H_j. To see primality directly, suppose uv belongs to p_j and u does not. Choose m>=1 with u^m v^m in H_j. Then u^m is not in H_j, and primaryness yields (v^m)^h in H_j for some h>=1, so v is in p_j. Thus every p_j is a homogeneous prime.

Group the H_j by equal radicals. For a nonempty group with common radical p, put K=intersection_j H_j. This is homogeneous and proper. Its radical is p: membership in radical K implies membership in every radical H_j; conversely for v in p choose v^{h_j} in H_j and take h=max_j h_j to obtain v^h in K. If uv is in K and u is not in K, choose j with u not in H_j. Primaryness gives v in p=radical K, hence a positive power of v in K. Thus K is primary. Replacing each group by K keeps the intersection I and gives distinct homogeneous prime radicals.

source.place: Theorem 20.27; Chapter 18, elementary combination of primary factors with the same radical.

proof.text: From the finite list of grouped factors repeatedly delete a factor whenever deleting it leaves the intersection unchanged. Each deletion strictly decreases the number of factors, so this terminates. The remaining list Q_1,...,Q_s still intersects to I, still has homogeneous proper primary factors and distinct radicals, and is irredundant by the stopping rule. Since I is proper the list is not empty.

Let p be any prime containing I. If no Q_a were contained in p, choose q_a in Q_a outside p for each a. The finite product of the q_a lies in every Q_a and hence I, yet is outside p by primality, a contradiction. Consequently some Q_a is contained in p. For x in p_a choose x^h in Q_a; since Q_a is contained in p, primality implies x in p. Therefore p_a is contained in p. If p is minimal among primes containing I, then I is contained in p_a, and p_a is prime by step 3, so p=p_a. This proves occurrence of every minimal prime.

source.place: Chapter 18, minimal primes of a finite primary decomposition; explicit finite-product argument.

proof.text: Fix a. Because B is Noetherian by step 1, the ideal p_a is finitely generated. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-fg-ideal-radical-power] to the ideals p_a and Q_a of B: the required containment p_a contained in radical Q_a is equality by definition. It gives h_a>=1 with p_a^{h_a} contained in Q_a.

source.place: Stacks Tag 00IM, lemma-Noetherian-power; finite-generation form of its proof.

proof.text: Fix a prime p containing I and S=B minus p. For an ideal J, a fraction r/s belongs to JB_p exactly when tr belongs to J for some t in S. Indeed the fractions j/u with j in J form an ideal (addition uses numerator vj+uj_prime, multiplication uses numerator bj), so they are exactly the extension of J. If r/s=j/u, the fraction equivalence in [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] supplies v in S with v(ur-sj)=0, whence vu r=vs j belongs to J. Conversely tr in J gives r/s=(tr)/(ts).

source.place: Chapter 12, localization membership; direct fraction argument from the definition.

proof.text: Extension is monotone, so IB_p is contained in every Q_aB_p. Conversely, if r/s lies in all Q_aB_p, step 8 gives t_a outside p with t_a r in Q_a. Put t=product_a t_a, still outside p; then tr lies in all Q_a and hence I, so r/s is in IB_p by step 8. Thus IB_p=intersection_a Q_aB_p. If p_a is not contained in p, choose z in p_a outside p. Some z^h lies in Q_a; it is invertible in B_p, so Q_aB_p=B_p. Removing exactly these unit factors proves the asserted localization formula.

source.place: Proposition 18.24 and Lemma 18.23, printed pp.109-110; explicit finite-denominator argument.

proof.text: If p=p_b is minimal over I and p_a is contained in p_b, then I is contained in the prime p_a, so minimality gives p_a=p_b. Distinctness of the radicals forces a=b. The localization formula therefore has the single remaining factor Q_bB_{p_b}, giving IB_{p_b}=Q_bB_{p_b}.

source.place: Theorem 18.25, printed p.110; specialization of the localization formula.

lean.statement: theorem homogeneous_primary_decomposition (k : Type u) [Field k] (n : ℕ) (I : Ideal (MvPolynomial (Fin (n + 1)) k)) (hI : @Ideal.IsHomogeneous _ _ _ _ _ _ (homogeneousSubmodule (Fin (n + 1)) k) _ _ gradedAlgebra I) : IsNoetherianRing (MvPolynomial (Fin (n + 1)) k) ∧ ∃ (s : ℕ) (Q : Fin s → Ideal (MvPolynomial (Fin (n + 1)) k)), I = ⨅ a, Q a ∧ (∀ a, Q a ≠ ⊤ ∧ @Ideal.IsHomogeneous _ _ _ _ _ _ (homogeneousSubmodule (Fin (n + 1)) k) _ _ gradedAlgebra (Q a) ∧ (Q a).IsPrimary ∧ (Q a).radical.IsPrime ∧ @Ideal.IsHomogeneous _ _ _ _ _ _ (homogeneousSubmodule (Fin (n + 1)) k) _ _ gradedAlgebra (Q a).radical) ∧ Function.Injective (fun a => (Q a).radical) ∧ (∀ a, (⨅ (b : Fin s) (_ : b ≠ a), Q b) ≠ I) ∧ (∀ p ∈ I.minimalPrimes, ∃ a, (Q a).radical = p) ∧ (∀ a, ∃ h : ℕ, 1 ≤ h ∧ (Q a).radical ^ h ≤ Q a) ∧ (∀ (p : Ideal (MvPolynomial (Fin (n + 1)) k)) [p.IsPrime], I ≤ p → I.map (algebraMap _ (Localization.AtPrime p)) = ⨅ (a : Fin s) (_ : (Q a).radical ≤ p), (Q a).map (algebraMap _ (Localization.AtPrime p)) ∧ (∀ a, ¬ (Q a).radical ≤ p → (Q a).map (algebraMap _ (Localization.AtPrime p)) = ⊤) ∧ (∀ b, p = (Q b).radical → I.IsMinimalPrime p → I.map (algebraMap _ (Localization.AtPrime p)) = (Q b).map (algebraMap _ (Localization.AtPrime p))))
